lesson.title: Spot the scam
lesson.subtitle: Five warning signs, and what to do next

video.title: Spot the scam
video.format_note: Animated explainer for students aged 12–16, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — maths teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice, talking to the student

scenes.visual: Classroom. Ms Salma holds up a student's phone: a chat message with sparkles and a login button. She raises one eyebrow.
scenes.narration: “Congratulations! You’ve won ten thousand game diamonds. Just log in here before midnight.” A student showed me this yesterday. Diamonds, a deadline and a login page. I’ve seen this film before.

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the cyber track chip.
scenes.narration: Today: how to spot a scam before it catches you, and what to do next.

scenes.visual: Message bubbles wrapped like gifts float through a game chat, a social feed and a text inbox.
scenes.animation: Bubbles drift in; one gift opens to show a hook.
scenes.narration: A scam is a message that tries to trick you into clicking, paying, or giving away a password or a code. Scammers go where young people are: game chats, social media, texts and WhatsApp. They use the games, the stars and the prizes you like.

scenes.visual: Five warning icons pop up one by one around a phone.
scenes.narration: Watch for five warning signs. It’s too good to be true. It hurries you. It asks for a code, a password or money. It has a link you didn’t expect. And the sender isn’t who they say they are.

scenes.visual: The diamonds message fills the screen; flags point at the prize, the deadline and the link.
scenes.animation: Flags pop as each sign is named.
scenes.narration: Look at the diamonds message again. Ten thousand free diamonds: too good to be true. Before midnight: a hurry. The login page isn’t the game’s own app, and that’s where they steal your password.

scenes.visual: Four scam cards flip in: a followers counter, a gift box with a fee, coins passing through a phone, a shop tag at half price.
scenes.animation: Cards flip in from the right.
scenes.narration: Other scams aimed at young people: “free followers” that need your password. Giveaways that want a small delivery fee. Easy money jobs that pass money through your account. And online shops with prices far too low, that want payment first.

scenes.visual: A raised hand, then a phone opening the official app, then a student asking a parent.
scenes.narration: So here’s the habit. Stop: don’t tap, reply or pay. Check another way: open the official app yourself, or ask a trusted adult. A real prize will still be there after you check.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds up a phone with a free data text.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A text says: “Free ten gigabytes of data! Tap here and enter your number and PIN.” Scam or safe?

scenes.visual: The scam card gets the check badge; a PIN pad locks with a shield.
scenes.on_screen_text: Your PIN is for you alone
scenes.narration: Scam. No real phone company asks for your PIN, and a free gift that needs it isn’t free. Your PIN is for you alone.

scenes.visual: Left: a flag, a block sign, a megaphone. Right: a student tells a parent; a heart.
scenes.narration: Spotted one? Don’t argue with the scammer: report it with the app’s report button, block the sender and warn your friends. Clicked or paid by mistake? Tell a trusted adult straight away: the sooner, the more can be saved. Being tricked doesn’t make you stupid: scammers do this all day.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma shows a social media shop post: a new phone at half price, pay first.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A shop on social media sells new phones at half price, but you must pay by mobile money first, today only. What do you do?

scenes.visual: Four summary cards: a warning sign, a raised hand, a phone checking, a flag.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: Don’t pay: half price, pay first and today only are three warning signs. Remember: spot the sign, stop, check another way, then report and tell.

scenes.visual: At home, a student scrolls a family phone with a parent and points at a suspicious message.
scenes.animation: Finger points; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: look through the messages on your phone, or a family phone with permission, and find one with a warning sign. Show it to someone at home, and explain which sign gave it away.

checkpoints.prompt: A text says: “Free 10 GB of data! Tap here and enter your number and PIN.” Scam or safe?

options.text: Scam — no real company asks for your PIN
Safe, if the link looks real

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — no real company asks for your PIN. A gift that needs it isn’t a gift.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a real phone company never asks for your PIN, and the link isn’t its website. Delete it and report it.

checkpoints.prompt: A social media shop sells new phones at half price. You must pay by mobile money first, today only. What do you do?

options.text: Pay fast, before the offer ends
Don’t pay — it shows three warning signs

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — half price, pay first and today only are all warning signs. Check with a trusted adult before any online payment.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a price far too low, payment first and a deadline are classic scam signs. Money sent by mobile money is hard to get back.
